opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

I think social robots will become one of the most important forms of what I call "physical AI," and probably the one closest to people's daily lives. For the past decade, most of our progress in AI has happened in the digital world: search, recommendation, and now large language models. But intelligence ultimately has to come into the physical world and interact with real people, and social robots are where those two things meet.

I see a few roles. The first and most urgent is companionship and care. China, Japan, Korea, and much of Europe are facing rapidly aging populations. We simply won't have enough caregivers. A social robot that can remind an elderly person to take medicine, notice if they've fallen, hold a conversation, and connect them with family or doctors could make a real difference. It doesn't replace human care, but it extends it.

The second is education. Children learn through interaction, and a robot tutor that is patient, adapts to each child, and is available any time could help a lot, especially in places where good teachers are scarce.

The third is service: in homes, hospitals, hotels, and public spaces. Here the robot is less a companion and more an assistant that understands context and speaks naturally.

What has changed recently is that large models give robots a real "brain." Before, social robots could only follow scripts, and people got bored quickly. Now they can understand language, emotion, and intent much better. The bottleneck has shifted to the body: dexterity, safety, cost, and battery life. I believe those will improve quickly over the next five to ten years.

But we have to be careful. When a machine becomes emotionally engaging, questions of trust, privacy, and dependency become very serious, especially for children and the elderly. A social robot should be transparent that it is a machine, it should protect personal data, and humans should always remain in control. So my view is optimistic, but with responsibility built in from the start. The goal is not to replace human relationships, but to give people more time, more dignity, and more connection.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's a pleasure to be here.

When I think about social robots, I actually like to step back and look at the bigger picture of what I call embodied intelligence. Over the past few years, we've seen large language models transform how machines understand and generate language. The next natural step is for that intelligence to move from the digital world into the physical world, to perceive, to act, and to interact with people in real environments. Social robots sit right at the heart of that transition.

I see them playing roles in a few areas. The first is companionship and care. Many societies, including China, are aging rapidly, and there simply won't be enough caregivers. A robot that can remind someone to take medication, notice if they've fallen, hold a conversation, or just provide a sense of presence can make a real difference in quality of life. The second is education. Children learn differently from a patient, personalized tutor that can adapt to their pace and emotional state, and robots can offer that at scale. The third is service, in hospitals, hotels, homes, and public spaces, where a robot can handle routine interactions and free people up for things that require human judgment and warmth.

That said, I want to be careful not to oversell the timeline. Building a robot that is socially intelligent is much harder than building a chatbot. It needs to understand context, read emotion, handle the physical unpredictability of the real world, and do all of that safely and reliably. We're making progress on perception, on multimodal models, on learning from human demonstration, but there are still fundamental challenges in generalization, in robustness, and in cost.

And there's a deeper question we should keep asking, which is what kind of relationship we want between humans and these machines. I believe the goal should be augmentation, not replacement. A social robot should enhance human connection, not substitute for it. If an elderly person ends up talking only to a robot instead of their family, we've failed. If the robot helps them stay independent and connected to the people they love, we've succeeded.

So my view is that social robots will become a meaningful part of daily life over the next decade or two, but the shape they take will depend as much on our values and design choices as on the technology itself. That's why I think this is such an exciting and important moment to be working in this field.

astra-6.text:
I think social robots will become companions and assistants in our everyday lives. Beyond performing physical tasks, they could help people learn, communicate, and stay connected. For an older person living alone, for example, a robot might provide reminders, help them reach family members, or simply offer some conversation.

But companionship requires more than intelligence. A robot needs to understand context, respond appropriately, and respect people's privacy. We also need to be careful that these systems support human relationships rather than replace them. To me, the most valuable role for social robots is helping people live more independently while staying connected to other people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think social robots will become an important part of how we interact with technology. Instead of always looking at a screen or typing commands, we’ll be able to communicate through speech, gestures, and more natural interaction.

One promising area is helping older people live independently—providing reminders, connecting them with family, and assisting with everyday tasks. Another is education, where a robot could support a teacher and adapt to a child’s pace of learning.

But we have to distinguish a useful companion from a replacement for human relationships. A social robot should help people connect with other people. And because it may operate in our homes, around children and older adults, privacy, safety, and trust have to be central to its design. The real measure of success is whether it improves someone’s daily life.
